title: Wellbeing and taking part
subject: PSHE
label: Public edition
objective_verbatim: World Mental Health Day, looking after my wellbeing.
calendar_note: Owner correction: the original World Mental Health Day hook (10 October) is outside Autumn 2. The teaching hook is International Day of Persons with Disabilities, 3 December, within Week 5. Keep the exact source objective, unit, accreditation and assessment in the source record. Disability and mental ill health are not synonyms; teach wellbeing and inclusive access without diagnosis or simulation.
assessment_verbatim: F: scenario sorting.  S: 'my trusted network' + safe/unsafe task (Dec).

sources.note: Current main bytes match the accepted unchanged source; workbook not redistributed.
W5 30 Nov–4 Dec; W6 7–11 Dec; W7 14–18 Dec. One lesson weekly per line; no day or slot inferred.

external_sources.title: Childline: Asking an adult for help
external_sources.supports: Choose a trusted adult, plan a message, use speech or a note, and seek another adult if needed. Adults may need to share a safety concern with people who can help.

external_sources.title: PSHE Association: Handling complex issues safely
external_sources.supports: Use ground rules, distanced examples, a right to pass and appropriate safeguarding responses.

external_sources.title: UN: International Day of Persons with Disabilities
external_sources.supports: Annual observance is 3 December. It promotes rights, wellbeing and participation. This is the owner-directed Week 5 hook; disability and mental ill health are not treated as synonyms.

evidence.description: An individual barrier/support match, a wellbeing step with reason, an available help route and a check of the learner’s chosen support.
evidence.status: contribution to source assessment; no completion claim

routes.Supported: Supported: choose from two support cards.
routes.Independent: Independent: explain a change and why.
routes.Aspire: Aspire: check if the person finds it useful.

vocab.definition: How we feel and manage day to day.
Something that makes taking part harder.
Being able to use or join something.
Make space for someone to take part.
Check what helped and what needs change.

cases.text: Jo cannot follow a long spoken task.
cases.next_step: Offer short steps in words and pictures.
cases.staff_note: Ask Jo which form is useful; do not infer a diagnosis.

cases.text: Sam finds the busy room too much.
cases.next_step: Ask staff about a quieter place or pause.
cases.staff_note: Use an agreed supervised option; do not send a pupil away alone.

cases.text: Lee wants to join a game but cannot use its usual controls.
cases.next_step: Ask Lee what would help; adapt the controls or role.
cases.staff_note: Avoid simulations of disability or assumptions about ability.

cases.text: Rae has a worry that keeps coming back.
cases.fact: The worry is not going away.
cases.next_step: Ask a trusted adult for a private talk.
cases.staff_note: A small wellbeing action is not a cure or replacement for support.

cases.text: Kit likes a short calm drawing break.
cases.fact: Kit has named a helpful activity.
cases.next_step: Agree a brief break and a return step.
cases.staff_note: Different people may choose different supports.

cases.text: An adult chooses help without asking Jo.
cases.next_step: Ask Jo what is wanted and check the effect.
cases.staff_note: Staff safety duties still apply; explain any limits respectfully.

The source assessment is retained. This lesson contributes evidence; it does not by itself complete an award. Public award labels are masked only.
Purpose and success checks
What could help me feel well and join in?
I can spot a barrier to taking part. I can choose a helpful change or support. I can explain one wellbeing step.
GROW-PSHE-W5-E1: An individual barrier/support match, a wellbeing step with reason, an available help route and a check of the learner’s chosen support.
Before pupils arrive

Print case cards and evidence sheets. Identify a quiet supervised option and available staff help. Offer simple visual steps and ordinary drawing materials; no disability simulation or diagnosis activity.
Offer processing time, a quiet start and the usual communication support. Capture each learner’s own work. Read the Staff Answers before teaching.

Access and practice
Supported: choose from two support cards. Independent: explain a change and why. Aspire: check if the person finds it useful.
Read A–F and model A. Pupils choose a case, match a support and explain why. Invite a small wellbeing step and check whether the learner wants it. Keep personal requests private.

Begin evidence during practice and finish during capture. Accept speech, pointing, drawing, writing or usual AAC. Scribe exact words without supplying the assessed reason. No forced pair work or public performance.
Safe teaching evidence and learner voice
Boundaries

Use fictional cases, role labels and a pass. No pupil must disclose health needs or family circumstances. Do not imply disability is a problem to fix; address barriers and respect choice. Follow the local safeguarding route for real concerns.
Assessment and feedback

Credit a specific barrier, a feasible helpful change and a reason linked to participation or wellbeing. Ask the person what helps; do not diagnose. A fictional plan is valid practice and must be labelled as such. Staff check the actual help route privately.

Retain actual work, response mode and support. Use VF · WS · I · NS+ (Yellow Box) · // (self-edit) · ? (read back) · R (responded) · E (evidence in the school's evidence record). R requires Voice, Audience, an NS+ prompt and the learner’s response in their own colour. Record E only after evidence is banked. Blank forms and adult models are not completed learner evidence.
Lundy moments
Space: calm, accessible participation. Voice: a choice, reason or help request. Audience: the adult listens or reads and replies. Influence: record the support or next-step change made in response.
Speaking listening and writing
Describe a barrier, request a change and listen to the person’s response. The receiving teacher maps authentic responses to their own portfolio; no communication criteria are assigned here.

These are possible responses and task guides, not learner observations. Accept a defensible answer based on the facts or actual work. Record each learner’s reasoning and support.

Model and hinge

Jo cannot follow a long spoken task. The adult asks what would help. Jo asks to see one step at a time. The adult gives a short visual guide. Jo can ask for a pause or more help. They check if the change helped Jo join in.

B. Listen to Jo and adapt the task so Jo can take part. Different support can give fair access. A ignores the barrier; C removes Jo’s voice. Reteach with a short instruction shown as a picture and words, then ask the learner which version helps.
Individual evidence key

Credit a specific barrier, a feasible helpful change and a reason linked to participation or wellbeing. Ask the person what helps; do not diagnose. A fictional plan is valid practice and must be labelled as such. Staff check the actual help route privately.
Feedback boundaries and next teaching
Card A: Ask Jo which form is useful; do not infer a diagnosis.
Card B: Use an agreed supervised option; do not send a pupil away alone.
Card C: Avoid simulations of disability or assumptions about ability.
Card D: A small wellbeing action is not a cure or replacement for support.
Card E: Different people may choose different supports.
Card F: Staff safety duties still apply; explain any limits respectfully.
Common misunderstandings

Fair access may require different support. Disability does not mean mental ill health. A calm activity may help someone but is not a cure, and a person should not have to disclose a diagnosis to ask for help.
Teaching boundary

Use fictional cases, role labels and a pass. No pupil must disclose health needs or family circumstances. Do not imply disability is a problem to fix; address barriers and respect choice. Follow the local safeguarding route for real concerns.
Feedback

If a reason is missing, return to the fact or actual work. Re-model a different example, then keep the learner’s own revision. Use NS+ and the learner response in their own colour before R. E means evidence actually banked. Keep safeguarding records separate.
Assessment boundary
GROW-PSHE-W5-E1 contributes to the source assessment. No criterion, registration or award completion is invented. Sources: FACTS_LEDGER.md.
